title: Redwood Private VPC security architecture deep dive with Mariner Capital

Focus on Mariner's requirement for SOC2-level auditability, strict egress controls, and customer-managed keys. Action items: share detailed network diagram, SOC 2 Type II report, and demonstration of KMS BYOK flow.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-02 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Samira Patel (Redwood Solutions Architect); Nina Rao (CISO, Mariner), Liam O'Connor (Head of Platform), Priya Shah (Security Eng), Marcus Lee (Network Arch)

Summary (auto): quick run through of network isolation patterns for Private Redwood deployment inside customer VPC, ingress/egress questions around outbound connections and software update channels, encryption and KMS options incl BYOK/HSM, audit log collection and retention, SOC2/ISO evidence expectations.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for making time. we wanted to do a deep dive on our private vpc architecture and how it maps to your network and security requirements. we know mariner has pretty strict egress rules so want to cover that up front.
[00:12] Nina: thanks avery, yeah, uh, we looked at the brief deck you sent, but main concerns are: where does data traverse, who holds keys, and how do we get audit logs into our siem without outbound holes.
[00:25] Diego: great, i'll start with a high level. Redwood Private runs a customer-dedicated control plane and inference capacity inside your VPC. there are two deployment patterns: a customer-managed VPC where our nodes are launched into your private subnets, or an air-gapped on-prem install. most banks usually pick the VPC pattern with tight egress controls.
[00:42] Liam: just to clarify, when you say "nodes launched into our subnets" do you need public IPs or nat? we have no public subnets in prod.
[00:48] Diego: no public IPs required. we recommend placing instances in private subnets, and using endpoints for aws s3 / cloudwatch / kinesis as needed. for the control plane communication we support connector patterns: either a reverse tls tunnel to a customer-controlled egress proxy, or a direct peering/transit-gateway model where we bring a small set of IPs into your routing table. both avoid assigning public ips.
[01:10] Marcus: ok, we do transit-gw for partner peering today. how do you handle route propagation and overlap with our existing route tables?
[01:18] Samira: in the transit model we ask for a /28 or /27 dedicated to redwood endpoints, and we'll advertise via the tgw. we also support prefix lists so you can restrict specific service endpoints. if there are conflicts we coordinate on specific subnets. most customers keep a dedicated AZ spread set of subnets for inference nodes.
[01:35] Priya: what about egress blocking — we want zero outbound except to a handful of approved endpoints. can we block updates/telemetry from reaching the internet?
[01:42] Diego: yes. we can lock egress to only your approved endpoints. our recommended pattern is to use vpc endpoints for internal services and allow egress only to these endpoints through firewall rules. for any outbound to redwood managed services (when needed) we provide an IP allowlist that you can host in your firewall, or we can run a private link so traffic never leaves aws backbone.
[02:00] Nina: for compliance we need all egress audited and tied to a ticket, also no unexpected DNS leakage. do you support DNS hijacking protections or forced dns resolvers?
[02:09] Samira: we recommend forcing AWS Route53 Resolver forwarding to your managed resolvers, and disallowing udp/53 egress elsewhere. our agents can be constrained to use the VPC resolver. we also log dns queries locally and push to your log collector over an approved channel. transcription note: sometimes agent side logs were labeled as "local logs" in the deck — hope that matches.
[02:29] Liam: key management — do we keep keys? BYOK? hsm? what's the lifecycle?
[02:34] Diego: we support multiple models. by default our private deployment can integrate with your KMS via aws-kms or on-prem hsm using PKCS#11. for object storage and disk encryption we can use customer-managed CMKs; for mTLS and ephemeral node keys we rotate locally and optionally escrow wrapped keys to your KMS. BYOK flow: you provision a CMK and grant the Redwood service principal decrypt/encrypt rights for the key; we only store wrapped keys and never plain-text. the HSM option is available for higher assurance — we have a documented flow for attestation and key import.
[03:05] Nina: do you support key rotation and split knowledge? our policy requires rotation every 90 days and separation of duties.
[03:12] Samira: yes, key rotation can be automated via your KMS policies; Redwood will call kms:GenerateDataKey or use kms:Encrypt for wrapping. for split knowledge we can do external wrapping where you maintain the unwrapping token in an HSM you control. we also support customer-supplied wrapped keys — basically you hold the root unwrap.
[03:28] Marcus: how about encryption in transit? mTLS? mutual auth?
[03:33] Diego: all control plane comms are TLS 1.3 with mutual TLS by default for node-to-control-plane. for data plane streams we support mTLS and optional application-level encryption for sensitive payloads. you can also terminate TLS at a customer-managed NLB if you want full control over certs.
[03:49] Priya: audit logs — we need immutable logs, tamper-evident, and a copy into our SIEM with at least seven years retention for certain buckets. how do you deliver?
[03:58] Samira: we push logs to customer owned S3 buckets via VPC endpoint or to a syslog endpoint over TLS. for immutability we recommend S3 Object Lock (governance mode) plus server-side encryption with your CMK. we can also stream to Kinesis Data Firehose to your SIEM. for tamper evidence we ship signed log bundles and maintain a hash chain; we also provide a signed audit report on request.
[04:22] Nina: is this all in your standard compliance pack? we need SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 artifacts before legal will sign.
[04:29] Avery: yes, we will share our SOC2 Type II report and ISO summary under an NDA. many customers require redaction — we have a standard procedure and can provide a security questionnaire.
[04:37] Liam: network firewalling specifics — do you require security group rules on our side? are there agent-level ports?
[04:44] Diego: typical agent ports are outbound 443 for control plane and optional 9000-9100 for internal metrics if you want direct scraping. but those are optional. we recommend security groups that allow ephemeral outbound to the approved endpoints and restrict inbound to the bastion/jump host. no inbound from internet to inference nodes. we also support host-based firewall policies (iptables/nft) baked into the AMIs to enforce least privilege.
[05:06] Marcus: we operate in a shared multi-account setup. can you support cross-account role assumption for deployment?
[05:12] Samira: yes, we do cross-account deploys. we ask for an IAM role in your target account with a narrow set of permissions; we do not require full admin. deployment runs under that role and provisioning is auditable in CloudTrail. we also support delegated admin models if your infra team prefers.
[05:29] Priya: logging latency — we need near-real time logs for detections. how quick are logs available in our SIEM?
[05:35] Diego: with Kinesis/Firehose you can have sub-minute delivery in most cases; with S3 batch uploads it's more like 1-5 minutes depending on buffer size. we can turn up the Firehose buffers for pilot to meet your detection SLAs.
[05:48] Nina: what about vulnerability scanning/patching of nodes? we have strict maintenance windows.
[05:53] Samira: we support customer-controlled patch windows. images are built and tested by Redwood; we push updates via your internal image pipeline or via scheduled maintenance windows. you control when updates are accepted. RA notes: some customers prefer immutable image swaps to reduce drift.
[06:10] Liam: can we run our own sidecars for traffic inspection, e.g. eBPF or envoy?
[06:15] Diego: yes, typically we allow a sidecar model where you can run an inspection sidecar. for high isolation we recommend a dedicated namespace per workload and node selector labeling to prevent co-location.
[06:27] Nina: data residency — we must ensure all customer data stays in eu-west-1 and never crosses regions. how do you ensure that?
[06:35] Diego: we deploy inference nodes into the specific region you choose and we do not replicate data cross-region unless explicitly configured. control plane metadata can be kept in your region with our private control plane deployment; if you need full air-gapped we can run an on-prem control plane. we'll include a region-lock SLA in the contract.
[06:52] Priya: incident response — do you offer playbooks and forensics access?
[06:57] Samira: yes, we provide an incident response runbook for private customers, and can grant time-bound forensic read-only access to logs and artifacts. we also offer joint post-mortem support for critical incidents.
[07:08] Marcus: one last thing — we have internal requirement for network allowlist only during business hours for debug. can you support time-bound egress exceptions?
[07:16] Diego: we can: either via a scheduled firewall rule change (you control) or we can coordinate with an automation runbook where we only open ports for a given time window and audit that change. we log all allowlist changes.
[07:28] Avery: ok, to recap the deliverables: we'll send the detailed network architecture and a SOC2 package, diego will prepare KMS BYOK demo, samira will coordinate the pilot kickoff. priya will share CIDRs and approved endpoints.
[07:40] Nina: thanks, this was helpful. please make sure the SOC2 redaction process is clear and we get the KMS workflow documented.
[07:46] Avery: will do. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the KMS workshop and pilot kickoff. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
